name: PT Lautan Luas Tbk

frontmatter.title: Lautan Luas at nine months: the margin moderated, the year did not
frontmatter.summary: Results note on PT Lautan Luas: BUY, target Rp1,604 from Rp885, a 87.8% return. The third quarter printed IDR3,091.0bn of revenue, 17.3% gross margin and IDR210.0bn of operating income: a sequential margin give-back in distribution, but the highest revenue quarter in the data we hold [S7]. We roll FY2026E to the filed nine months plus a flat fourth quarter, lifting revenue to IDR11,291.5bn and earnings per share to Rp192 [S6][S7].
thesis: The third quarter printed IDR3,091.0bn of revenue and IDR210.0bn of operating income, so the nine months reached IDR8,200.8bn and IDR558.8bn against IDR6,425.0bn and IDR308.0bn a year earlier, with the gross margin at 18.5% against 15.7% for the whole of FY2025 [S2][S6][S7]. We roll FY2026E to that filed nine months plus a fourth quarter held at the third quarter's level: revenue of IDR11,291.5bn, 28.3% growth, EBITDA of IDR956.4bn and attributable profit of IDR281.0bn, with the tax rate blended to the filed nine-month charge [S6][S7].
Our primary DCF values the share at Rp1,803; the probability-weighted, liquidity-adjusted twelve-month value is Rp1,604, and the base scenario alone is worth Rp2,059 [S0].

The through-cycle DCF carries the whole of the value, at 100% of the blend. The peer EV/EBITDA multiple is kept as a cross-check rather than a weighted leg: the engine applies one fixed minority deduction to every method, and a claim calibrated on the DCF's own pre-minority equity removes close to half of the much smaller equity base of the multiple leg, so that leg prints a floor well below what its own arithmetic implies — a defect one bridge item and two equity bases cannot calibrate away. A P/E on the same trough profit would measure the impairments and the minority mix rather than the cycle, and the dividend-capacity anchor stays an unweighted cross-check because a forward payout over a trailing peer yield imports the same trough defect [S0][S5].

The balance sheet is valued, not waved at: associates at IDR653.3bn are carried at zero in the bridge because their losses are modelled inside the group, the listed equity instruments at IDR353.7bn are added at their quoted value, investment properties at IDR452.3bn stay out because their rent already sits in the EBITDA we discount, and the minority is deducted at a capitalised value rather than its IDR314.6bn book; parent equity is IDR3,461.7bn [S6].

What tempers the call is liquidity and control: PT Caturkarsa Megatunggal holds 56.6% and the public 36.1%, with treasury stock at 6.1%, and three-month average daily value traded is IDR203.0m, so the engine strips 20.0% from the weighted value before setting the target [S10][S0].
The risk that matters is a faster reversal of chemical and plastics prices than the Brent deck assumes, with import competition already visible in the industry association's complaints [S12].

catalysts.event: Maturity of the series B bond due this month — the first half of the refinancing test; the company says it has scheduled the payment, and no repayment announcement had been made when this note was written, so the test remains the price and tenor of the replacement [S9][S2]
FY2026 audited accounts and annual report — the first full year carrying the restated depreciation base, a full year of the 2026 price gains and the fourth quarter this note holds flat [S5]
Maturity of the 2024 series bonds in July 2027 — the second refinancing test [S5]
Gross margin and working capital cycle: the two lines that decide whether the nine-month gain holds [S2][S7]

blocks.text: We update PT Lautan Luas on the third-quarter filing with a BUY rating and a twelve-month target of Rp1,604, against a price of Rp885 on the last close we hold. Including the dividend we expect over the period, Rp58 a share, the expected total return is 87.8% [S0].

What the quarter changed is the base, not the case. Revenue of IDR3,091.0bn in the three months to September was the highest quarter in the data we hold, against IDR2,858.0bn in the second, and it carried the nine months to IDR8,200.8bn, 27.6% ahead of the same period last year on both volumes and selling prices [S7][S2]. The margin, though, gave back what the second quarter had gained: 17.3% gross margin in the third quarter against 20.7% in the second, a moderation the company puts on the distribution segment, with operating income of IDR210.0bn and attributable profit of IDR71.0bn [S7]. We therefore roll FY2026E onto a filed base — the nine months plus a fourth quarter held flat on the third — which gives revenue of IDR11,291.5bn, 28.3% growth, EBITDA of IDR956.4bn and earnings per share of Rp192 [S6][S7]. The target moves down from the previous note even though the earnings move up, because the bridge now deducts the minority at what it earns rather than at its book and carries the associate book at zero; the rating does not move, because the discount that produces it is the same discount.

The market is valuing a business that earned IDR149.5bn for its owners in FY2025 at 8.7x those earnings and 0.4x parent book value, even though the first nine months of 2026 have already produced IDR195.6bn of attributable profit and operating income of IDR558.8bn against IDR308.0bn a year earlier [S2][S6]. That is a step up in operating income, not a doubling of the operating margin: most of the gain is the gross margin recovering from a trough while operating expenses grew more slowly than revenue, and we do not extrapolate either leg [S6][S2]. We do not think the market is missing the results; the shares trade at Rp885 [S0]. What the price is doing, in our reading, is refusing to capitalise a cyclical margin at anything like a normal multiple for a company with a thin free float, a controlling shareholder and a bond wall to refinance [S5][S7].

Three things shape the call. The first is the earnings reset: revenue of IDR8,200.8bn in the nine months to September 2026 is 27.6% higher than a year earlier, operating income reached IDR558.8bn against IDR412.7bn for the whole of FY2025, and the gross margin of 18.5% came with a working capital cycle of 52.0 days rather than a build [S2][S6]. The second is the balance sheet, which we value item by item rather than treating as support: the associates of IDR653.3bn are carried at zero because the losses they absorb are already modelled inside the group, the listed equity instruments of IDR353.7bn are added at their quoted value, the investment properties of IDR452.3bn are excluded because their rent already sits in the EBITDA we discount, and the minority is deducted at a capitalised value rather than the IDR314.6bn book [S6]. The third is what we deliberately give back: because the shares are illiquid, the engine takes 20.0% off the probability-weighted value before the target is set, which is why the target is Rp1,604 rather than the Rp2,005 the scenarios average to [S0].

Our primary method is a ten-year discounted cash flow at a weighted average cost of capital of 12.0%, and it produces Rp1,803 a share. It carries 100% of the value. We do not weight a peer multiple into it. The engine can only read the data pack's last-twelve-months series, which falls back to FY2025 — the trough year, with EBITDA of IDR559.2bn on a 15.7% gross margin [S0][S5] — and, decisively, it applies one fixed rupiah minority deduction to every method: a claim struck on the DCF's pre-minority equity removes close to half of the EV/EBITDA leg's much smaller equity base, so that leg prints a floor well below what its own arithmetic implies. With one bridge item and two equity bases the error cannot be calibrated per leg, so the method whose minority deduction is exact is the method that values the company; the previous version weighted the multiple as a residual leg and understated the target for exactly this reason. The multiple is still reported in the valuation section as a cross-check on the same trough EBITDA, and the trough case remains the floor of the range even though it does not enter the blend. The dividend-capacity anchor is likewise a cross-check, and a P/E on the same trough profit would capitalise the impairments booked above the operating line and the minority mix, so it is not used at all [S5][S6]. The valuation section works through the basis effect rather than hiding it.

What would make us wrong is not a bad quarter but a bad cycle. The industry association says petrochemical and plastics producers are under pressure from cheaper imports and is asking the ministry for safeguard and anti-dumping measures [S12]. If chemical prices roll over faster than the Brent deck assumes, the nine-month margin compresses toward the FY2025 trough, and our bear case of Rp316 is the honest marker of that path.

PT Lautan Luas is an integrated ingredients and solutions provider that began as an importer of basic and specialty chemicals and now runs three segments: distribution, manufacturing, and support and services [S7]. Distribution takes chemical products from international principals and delivers them to Indonesian industry; manufacturing makes specialty chemicals and ingredients, including water-treatment chemicals; and the support and services segment sells technical services, warehousing and water-treatment solutions around the products [S7][S10].

The segment mix is the key to the economics. In FY2025 distribution produced external revenue of IDR4,513.9bn, manufacturing IDR3,695.8bn and support and services IDR589.4bn. The profit pool is weighted differently: distribution earned segment gross profit of IDR617.7bn, manufacturing IDR699.6bn and services IDR124.7bn [S5]. Manufacturing therefore converts a smaller revenue base into a larger gross profit than distribution, and services, though small, earns the widest margin of the three. By the third quarter of 2026 the mix had shifted slightly toward manufacturing: distribution was 49.0% of revenue, manufacturing 45.0% and support and services 6.0%, against a FY2025 split in which distribution was still above half [S2][S5].

The distribution business is the scale engine. It is supported by more than a hundred international principals and over a thousand products, spread across Indonesia, Singapore, Shanghai, Thailand and Vietnam, and serves food and beverages, animal feed, water, personal care, agriculture, mining, plastics and rubber [S7]. In Indonesia it operates through four branches, five representative offices and one bonded warehouse [S2]. That footprint is the asset: a principal that wants national coverage of a thousand product lines in a market with fragmented regional distributors is buying reach, bonded inventory and technical support, not just a purchase order.

Manufacturing is where the capital and the margin sit. The group runs seven manufacturing subsidiaries and four support and services subsidiaries [S2]. The water-treatment franchise is the strategic piece: the partnership with Organo Corporation of Japan dates from 2013, and in April 2025 the company raised its ownership of PT Lautan Organo Water from a minority position to a controlling majority, taking control and consolidating it [S10]. That transaction explains part of the year-on-year step in revenue and in minority interest, and it is why the water and chemicals businesses are named as the growth drivers in the 2026 plan [S2][S10]. Its arithmetic is small: the support and services segment where LOW sits was 6.7% of FY2025 revenue and grew 13.5% that year, so even if the whole of that segment's growth were the consolidation it would add only a fraction of a percentage point to the 27.6% nine-month revenue growth [S10][S2]. The step is therefore organic — volume and price — not a consolidation artefact, and the FY2027E growth rate in our model is struck off a base that already contains a full year of LOW.

The company's own plan for 2026, set at the end of 2025, targeted revenue growth of 7.0% to 9.0% and an attributable net margin of 1.5% to 3.0% of revenue, with net interest-bearing debt to equity projected at about 0.4x — the last of these a capital-structure target rather than a forecast [S10]. The first nine months have already beaten the revenue target, which tells us the plan underestimated the price effect in chemicals rather than that management is sandbagging.

Control is concentrated. PT Caturkarsa Megatunggal is both the immediate parent and the ultimate parent of the group and holds 56.6% of the shares; two directors, Pranata Hajadi and Indrawan Masrin, hold 0.6% and 0.6%; treasury stock is 6.1%; and the public holds 36.1% [S10]. The company employs 3,143 people [S0]. We treat the controlling shareholder as permanent, not as a seller, and value the minority stake accordingly.

Chemical distribution in Indonesia is a relationship and logistics business before it is a manufacturing business. The distributor's edge comes from holding exclusive or semi-exclusive principal mandates, from carrying the working capital that lets it hold stock in bonded warehouses, and from technical service that helps customers reformulate. Manufacturing of specialty chemicals and water-treatment chemistry sits on top of that network, earns a wider margin and consumes more capital. Global majors have generally chosen to reach Indonesian industry through local partners rather than build their own distribution, which is the structural reason a company of this kind can earn a return above its cost of capital through a cycle even when commodity chemical prices are falling.

The demand backdrop improved through 2026. The chemicals, pharmaceuticals and traditional medicine industry grew 8.1% in the third quarter of 2026, according to the government's growth briefing, driven by the completion of chemical-sector investments and by pharmaceutical expansion to supply the national health programme [S11]. That matters for Lautan Luas because its distribution book sells into exactly those chains: food ingredients, personal and home care, water treatment, and basic and specialty chemicals are the four drivers the company names for 2026 [S10].

The same industry is under import pressure. The plastics and petrochemical association says producers are being squeezed by cheaper imported product and has asked the Ministry of Industry for safeguard and anti-dumping measures, while the minister has promised protection through standards and trade remedies [S12]. This cuts both ways for a distributor. Cheaper imports lower the price of what it sells, which compresses revenue per tonne and can force inventory write-downs; but a distributor with principal relationships and technical service earns a margin on the service and the bundle, and is less exposed to the domestic producer's cost position than a manufacturer would be. The risk is real in the commodity end of the range, where price is the only differentiator.

The demand drivers are worth separating. Water treatment is the most structural: Indonesian industrial and municipal water infrastructure is under-built, and the group's Organo partnership puts it inside the technical specification of new plants rather than at the commodity end of the market [S10]. Food ingredients and personal care are volume businesses with reformulation service attached, where a distributor's application laboratory is the differentiator [S7][S10]. Agriculture and mining are cyclical and price-sensitive. Plastics and rubber are the most exposed to import competition and to the oil price [S12].

On competitive position, we would characterise Lautan Luas as the scale incumbent in Indonesian chemical distribution rather than a price-setter. Its advantages are the breadth of principal relationships, the product range, the national logistics footprint and the bonded warehouse, and the technical service capability in water and food [S7][S2]. Its disadvantages are that it does not own the brands it distributes, that principals can and do appoint second distributors, and that its customers are large industrial buyers with purchasing power. The result is a business that earns a distribution margin in the low teens on the traded book and a manufacturing margin in the high teens on its own products, with returns that depend on volume and working capital discipline rather than on pricing power [S5].

Five forces, briefly. Supplier power is high and rising: the principals own the product and the brand, and the distributor's switching cost runs the other way. Buyer power is moderate to high in food and personal care, where customers are large and can multi-source, and lower in water treatment, where the specification and service relationship bind. The threat of new entrants is moderate in distribution, because working capital and principal relationships are barriers, and low in water-treatment chemistry, where process know-how and the Organo relationship matter. Substitutes are a slow force: formulators can change a chemical input, but the service bundle usually survives the substitution. Rivalry is intense in commodity chemicals and moderate in specialty [S5][S12].

The macro deck sets the frame for costs. The rupiah is at Rp18,228/USD against the dollar at the time of writing, while the deck's average for FY2026E is Rp17,570/USD, so imported chemical costs are translating at a weaker rate than the year's average, and Brent is put at US$96.0/bbl for FY2026E, falling through the deck's explicit years to US$78.0/bbl by FY2029 and a little lower again in FY2030 and then escalating again toward the mid-eighties by FY2035, above the deck's long-run marker of US$75.0/bbl [d.macro][d.oil.brent]. A distributor passes most of that through with a lag; what it cannot pass through is the working capital cost of carrying inventory whose replacement cost is falling [S7][S5].

The structural feature of this industry is that the distributor's return on capital is driven by inventory turns and receivable days, not by gross margin alone. A percentage point of gross margin is worth less than a week of working capital cycle when volumes are growing, because the funding cost of receivables and stock is carried on the distributor's balance sheet while the principal keeps the brand. That is why the companies that survive cycles are the ones with the widest principal mandates and the tightest credit control, and why the market watches working capital days as closely as the margin.

The first thing to fix in the historical data is depreciation. The data pack originally carried FY2025 D&A at roughly a third of the audited figure. The accounts allocate IDR146.6bn of fixed-asset depreciation across cost of goods sold, services, selling and general expenses, so we restate the line from the notes for FY2024 and FY2025; that is why FY2025 D&A in our model is IDR146.6bn and FY2024 EBITDA is IDR571.0bn rather than the pack's lower numbers [S5]. Right-of-use depreciation of IDR50.2bn and intangible amortisation of IDR0.5bn are disclosed separately and excluded from the engine line so that the cash-flow add-back matches the fixed-asset roll-forward [S5].

FY2025 was a trough year on the income statement. Revenue of IDR8,799.2bn produced a gross margin of 15.7%, EBITDA of IDR559.2bn and attributable profit of IDR149.5bn, or Rp102 a share on the current share count [S5]. The margin was squeezed because cost of goods sold grew faster than revenue, and the operating result was held up by other operating income of IDR94.3bn against other operating expenses of IDR68.2bn — a net contribution that is the gap between gross profit less operating expenses and the reported operating income [S5]. We show the reported operating income of IDR412.7bn in the model and calibrate the opex ratio so that forecasts are struck on the same basis.

The first nine months of 2026 changed the picture. Revenue of IDR8,200.8bn generated gross profit of IDR1,516.4bn, operating income of IDR558.8bn and attributable profit of IDR195.6bn against IDR120.0bn, with company-reported EBITDA of IDR665.0bn against IDR421.0bn a year earlier [S6][S2][S7]. The gross margin of 18.5% is nearly three percentage points above the FY2025 level, and operating expenses grew far more slowly than revenue, so the operating margin expanded from both ends [S2][S6]. This is the one calibration gap in the model worth naming: our FY2026E EBITDA margin of 8.5% sits above the FY2025 audited 6.4% because it is built on the nine-month actual of IDR665.0bn on IDR8,200.8bn rather than on the trough year; holding the forecast at the FY2025 margin would contradict the filing. Part of the operating expense line in the nine months is one-off: other operating expenses of IDR68.2bn in FY2025 became a much larger charge in the nine months of 2026 after impairments of an associate, of other receivables and of amounts due from related parties, which is why our FY2026E operating expense ratio of 11.4% is above the 11.1% we hold thereafter [S6].

The quarter is worth reading line by line, because it is now the base of the forecast. The nine months alone are IDR8,200.8bn of revenue — most of a full year — and IDR558.8bn of operating income, above the IDR412.7bn the whole of FY2025 produced, so the year is running ahead of the forecast we published at initiation and the roll raises it rather than trimming it [S6][S5]. Third-quarter revenue of IDR3,091.0bn followed IDR2,858.0bn in the second without a step back, and the mix moved only slightly — distribution at 49.0% of revenue, manufacturing at 45.0% and support and services at 6.0% — so the growth is the same business at higher volumes and prices rather than a reallocation between segments [S2][S7]. What did move was the margin: 17.3% in the third quarter against 20.7% in the second, with the quarter's IDR210.0bn of operating income taking the nine months to IDR558.8bn against IDR308.0bn for the same period a year earlier and attributable profit of IDR71.0bn in the quarter alone [S7]. The roll we apply is exactly that: the filed nine months plus one quarter repeating the third, which gives IDR11,291.5bn of revenue, a 18.2% gross margin, IDR768.3bn of operating income and IDR281.0bn attributable to the parent [S6][S7]. We do not bank the normal fourth-quarter step — in 2025 the fourth quarter was stronger than the third — because that seasonality is one year of evidence and the price gains are newer than it [S0][S13][S7].

Two lines in the filing do the quiet work. The tax charge carries the first-half impairments, which are not deductible, and the associate losses are permanent and non-deductible, so the model carries 31.6% in every forecast year rather than dropping back to the statutory rate: the effective rate has run above the statutory line in each of the last two fiscal years and again in the nine months [S6][S5]. And cash: operating cash flow of IDR175.6bn in the nine months against attributable profit of IDR195.6bn is better than FY2025's IDR128.7bn for the full year but still behind the profit, which is why FY2026E free cash flow to the firm of IDR-27.3bn is thin and why the fourth quarter's working capital is the number to watch [S6][S5].

Our forecast builds revenue of IDR11,291.5bn for FY2026E, growing 28.3%, then IDR11,743.1bn and IDR12,330.3bn as growth settles to 4.0% and 5.0% [S0][S10]. The deceleration is our own judgement, not an engine output: revenue is not linked to the oil price in this model, so no part of the growth build is attributed to the deck. It is anchored on the revenue history in the accounts through the FY2025 trough, which compounds at a low single-digit rate over three years, and on a one-year plan that targeted growth in the high single digits [S10][S5]. We take the first plan year and then fade it, because the 2026 gain is partly the price of what the company distributes rather than volume it controls. The margin, not the top line, is where the outer years do their work, and it is where the deck bites: we treat 40.0% of cost of goods sold as Brent-exposed and 95.0% of any move as passed through in price, and a second link treats 35.0% of cost of goods sold as rupiah-exposed with 90.0% pass-through, which is the imported share of the purchase book net of the local manufacture [S5][d.oil.brent][d.macro]. Both links are struck at base input costs, so the delivered margin is the margin we intend rather than the margin after an unintended drag. After the links the effective margin is 18.2% in FY2026E and 17.8% in FY2027E, settling near the four-year mean rather than at the 2026 peak [S5][S7].

The earnings path follows: EBIT of IDR768.3bn, IDR786.8bn and IDR795.3bn, EBITDA of IDR956.4bn in FY2026E, attributable profit of IDR281.0bn and earnings per share of Rp192, rising to Rp197 [S0]. Dividends at a 30.0% payout are Rp58 for FY2026E against Rp31 paid for FY2025 [S5, S7]. Minority interests are forecast at 29.2% of net profit, the nine-month 2026 actual rather than the FY2025 trough-year share, because the manufacturing subsidiaries where the minorities sit are now the profit engine and nothing in the filing shows that mix reversing [S5][S6].

Cash conversion is the weak spot. FY2025 operating cash flow was IDR128.7bn against capital expenditure of IDR215.3bn and a working capital build that took operating working capital from IDR756.3bn to IDR1,139.1bn, so free cash flow to the firm was negative [S5]. The nine months of 2026 repeated the pattern in the balance sheet even as the working capital cycle improved: receivables of IDR1,804.6bn, inventories of IDR1,509.5bn and payables of IDR1,668.7bn plus IDR23.5bn to related parties [S6]. Our model assumes operating working capital at 14.2% of revenue, consistent with the 52.0 days cycle, which means FY2026E absorbs another working capital outflow before the cash flow normalises [S2].

The balance sheet is where the risk concentrates. At the end of September 2026 the company had interest-bearing debt of Rp1,523bn and cash of IDR354.8bn, net debt to EBITDA of 1.3x, and a current ratio of 1.1x [S6][S7][S2]. Within the current stack sit short-term bank loans of IDR860.4bn and bonds of IDR419.2bn classified as current, against current assets of IDR4,136.2bn and current liabilities of IDR3,586.5bn [S6]. The bonds themselves are unsecured: Rp135bn of series B notes mature in November 2026 and Rp286bn of the 2024 series in July 2027 [S5]. The company says it has scheduled the payment of the November maturity, and the improvement in net debt to EBITDA to 1.3x over the year shows the operating cash is there; the question is the price and tenor of the refinancing, not the ability to pay [S9][S2].

Capital allocation has been shareholder-friendly but modest. Dividends paid were IDR65.9bn in FY2025 and IDR52.0bn in FY2024, a payout at the 30.0% level the model holds, and the buyback programme that ran from September 2023 to February 2025 repurchased 90.2m shares at an average price well above today's Rp885 [S10][S5]. With capital expenditure at 2.5% of revenue — the FY2025 investment of IDR215.3bn, no disclosed budget for the current years and assets under construction not yet commissioned — there is no large project absorbing the cash, so the choice is between debt reduction, a higher dividend and acquisitions; the model assumes debt held flat and lets cash accumulate, which is the neutral assumption rather than a prediction [S10][S5].

On earnings quality we flag four things. First, cash conversion: profit has run ahead of operating cash flow for two years because working capital grows with revenue, which is normal for a distributor but leaves no cushion if growth stops [S5]. Second, the associate book: the share of losses was IDR44.3bn in FY2025 and IDR52.4bn in the nine months of 2026, and the company impaired an associate in both periods, so the IDR653.3bn carrying value is not a certain asset [S5][S6]. Third, the minority share of profit jumped from a low base in FY2025 to a much higher share in the nine months of 2026, which reduces the value of each rupiah of group profit to the parent's holders [S5][S6]. Fourth, the non-operating lines are volatile — gains on asset sales, dividend income, impairments of receivables and of related-party balances — and we have normalised rather than extrapolated them [S5][S6].

We use a discounted cash flow as the primary method because the value of this business is the cash it generates after the working capital it must fund, and because a distributor's earnings multiple is a poor guide when the margin is at a cyclical peak or trough. The cost of capital build follows the engine exactly: it starts from a risk-free rate of 7.4%, deducts the Indonesian default spread of 1.6% that the macro deck carries, adds a levered beta of 1.72 multiplied by the sum of the mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2% and the country risk premium of 2.5%, and then adds no separate illiquidity premium — illiquidity is charged once, through the traded-value discount applied to the target, not twice in the same number [S0][d.macro]. The beta is the industry unlevered beta of 0.90 relevered on gross interest-bearing debt against market capitalisation, a ratio of 1.17, which is high because the debt stack is large against a small market capitalisation; cash is removed in the equity bridge rather than netted off the debt weight, which is the textbook treatment [S0]. That gives a cost of equity of 17.4%. Debt costs 9.4% before tax, and at weights of 46.0% equity and 54.0% debt the weighted average cost of capital is 12.0%.

The DCF produces an enterprise value of IDR4,545.4bn and an equity value of Rp1,803 a share. The terminal value is 49.7% of enterprise value, which is high but not extreme for a ten-year horizon; the first explicit year contributes little because FY2026E absorbs a working capital build larger than the year's free cash flow [S0]. The bridge from enterprise to equity uses the 30 September 2026 balance sheet restated from the filing, and it is the part of the valuation where judgement matters most, so we set it out line by line [S6].

It subtracts net debt: IDR1,523.0bn of interest-bearing debt less IDR354.8bn of cash. It subtracts the minority, and here we depart from the house default of book value. The IDR314.6bn non-controlling interest took 29.2% of the group's operating profit in the nine months, because the manufacturing subsidiaries where it sits are the ones that recovered; deducting it at book would hand the parent a share of value the minority earns, and the gap is not small — the capitalised figure in the table is several times the book. We therefore deduct the minority at the value its share of the operating business implies, and we say what that costs: the capitalised figure is several times the book, the assumptions record sets out the arithmetic line by line, and the difference between the two is what a book deduction would add to our value — a material slice of it, and the single largest reason our number sits where it does rather than higher [S6].

It adds the associates at zero rather than at their IDR653.3bn carrying value. Their losses sit below the operating line at -70bn a year in every forecast year and are therefore excluded from the free cash flow the DCF discounts, so an associate added at book would be an asset whose cost of ownership is left out of the value. Carrying the book and deducting the discounted loss stream gives almost the same answer as zero, and zero is the more honest of the two, because the book has already been impaired twice for exactly this reason and we do not want the model to imply that a third impairment is impossible [S6][F66]. It adds the listed equity instruments at IDR353.7bn, their quoted value, because they are not in the earnings we capitalise: any change in their fair value sits in other comprehensive income rather than in profit, and the dividends they pay land in finance income, which the model does not carry [S6]. It leaves the investment properties of IDR452.3bn out, because their rental income is booked in other operating income and is therefore already inside the EBITDA the DCF discounts; adding their book as well would double count [S6].

We weight one method and report three cross-checks, and say what each is for. The DCF is the value: Rp1,803 a share at 100% of the blend, because it is the only instrument that capitalises the whole cycle rather than one year of it. The first cross-check is the peer-median EV/EBITDA multiple applied to the data pack's last-twelve-months EBITDA, which falls back to FY2025 — the trough year, IDR559.2bn — through the same September bridge [S0][S5]. It is deliberately not weighted, and the reason is mechanical rather than a view on the cycle: the engine applies one fixed rupiah minority deduction to every method, and a claim calibrated on the DCF's pre-minority equity removes close to half of the multiple leg's smaller equity base, so the leg prints a floor well below the value its own equity base implies. Weighting it would import that error into the target; the fix is to let the method whose deduction is exact carry the value, and to read the multiple as a floor, which is what the method card asks a current-year multiple to be for a cyclical [S0][S6]. The second cross-check is the dividend-capacity anchor: the next-twelve-month payout of Rp58 against the peer median yield, unweighted because dividing a forward dividend by a trailing peer yield mixes the cycle the same way. The third is the price itself, which the last paragraph of this section closes on.

Why the multiple is a cross-check and not a weighted leg. Two reasons, and the second is decisive. First, the peer multiples the engine holds are trailing multiples of the peers' own last reported year [S0]. Pairing a trailing peer multiple with our forward earnings would value next year's profit on the peers' current rating, which is the procyclical error the industry method card bans; the internally consistent pairing is trailing with trailing, and trailing means the trough. Second, the engine applies one fixed rupiah bridge item to every method. The minority claim is 29.2% of the DCF's pre-minority equity, but the EV/EBITDA leg's pre-minority equity is a fraction of the DCF's, because the trough EBITDA it capitalises is roughly a third of the through-cycle cash flow the DCF discounts; the same rupiah therefore removes close to half of it instead of a bit over a quarter. The leg prints a floor well below what a proportional deduction would give, and no single rupiah item can be right for two different equity bases. On our FY2026E EBITDA the same peer median produces a value within a tenth of the DCF — which is what we would expect, since FY2026E's margin is close to the four-year mean rather than to the trough — but we do not weight it, because it would be a trailing multiple on forward earnings and because its minority deduction is the wrong size [S0][S5]. The P/E leg is set to zero for a related reason: FY2025 attributable profit is distorted both by the trough margin and by the impairments booked inside other operating expenses above the operating line, and by a minority share that has since risen, so it measures neither the cycle nor the equity holder's claim on it [S5][S6]. The value that emerges from the DCF is Rp1,803.

The scenarios are mirrored around the base, driver for driver, and each of them can lose money — which the previous version of this note could not say. The bear cuts revenue growth by two points, takes two points off the delivered gross margin, reprices the debt stack nearly a third higher at the refinancing and weakens the rupiah five per cent against the dollar; the bull adds the same two points of growth and of margin, prices the refinancing nearly a third lower and strengthens the rupiah by the reciprocal. The probabilities are 50.0% base, 30.0% bear and 20.0% bull: the bear carries more odds than the bull because the third quarter already gave back part of the second quarter's margin gain and imports are pressing the commodity end, while the bull needs both the margin to hold and the refinancing to come in cheaper [S7][S12]. The values run from Rp316 in the bear through Rp2,059 to Rp4,404 [S0]. Three caveats we would rather state than bury. First, the bull's rupiah gain is larger than the bear's rupiah loss even though the driver shocks are equal and opposite: that is operating leverage in a ten-year DCF with a terminal value, and it is the reason the base case, not the bull, carries the rating. The bull still contributes roughly two-fifths of the probability-weighted value; we show that rather than let the average hide it. Second, the shocks move the growth rate rather than the revenue level, because the engine's scenario machinery can only shock an input series, so a two-point growth shock compounds into a wider revenue spread over ten years than it would in year one; we halved it from the previous version for that reason and we do not claim the tails are proportional in money. Third, the capitalised minority in the bridge is a fixed rupiah amount struck on the base-case DCF, so in the bear it deducts more than a proportional share of a smaller business and in the bull less of a larger one; the two errors partly offset in the weighted value, but the tails are directional rather than precise. Because the DCF now carries the whole weight, the method that sets the value has one equity base and its deduction in the base case is exactly the capitalised figure — the number we defend line by line — and the item is re-struck whenever that pre-minority equity moves, so it cannot drift into being 29.2% of nothing [S6].

The method card for this industry asks for a dividend-capacity anchor alongside the NAV, and the two point in different directions, which is the whole point. Our FY2026E dividend of Rp58 at a 30.0% payout is a yield of 6.5% at today's price and 6.7% on our FY2027E forecast. Capitalised at our DCF value, the same dividend is a yield roughly a third as large, so the market at Rp885 is valuing the share on its dividend stream, not on the cash flow the DCF sees: the dividend-capacity anchor is what the price is using, and the through-cycle NAV is what we use. The gap is the re-rating we are underwriting, and it will not close until the leverage that sits between the two falls. Net debt of IDR1,523.0bn of interest-bearing debt less IDR354.8bn of cash is a little over twice the FY2025 trough EBITDA of IDR559.2bn — the number the bond market will look at when the November maturity is refinanced [S6][S5].

What the price implies is the most useful cross-check we have. At Rp885 the shares change hands at 4.6x our FY2026E earnings and 3.0x our FY2026E EBITDA, so the market is valuing the operating business at a little over half of the peer median EBITDA multiple on earnings it has already begun to deliver [S0][S6][S7]. The reverse DCF cannot bracket that price inside the engine's solve range, which is itself the answer: to get from our cash flows to today's price requires a discount rate far above the one the balance sheet and the beta support, or a permanent reversal in the margin. We think the market is applying a governance and liquidity discount larger than the 20.0% we apply, and we say so plainly rather than dress it up as a fundamental view [S0]. That discount is a house parameter set by the traded-value schedule, not state-dependent in our target construction: we take it off every scenario, including the bull, because the shares turn over IDR203.0m a day and a position cannot be built or exited at NAV. What would retire it is turnover rising through the house threshold, which depends on the register — 36.1% public and 6.1% treasury stock today — not on the earnings; until then the bull case expresses the re-rating through the earnings and the cost of capital, and the discount stands.

Finally, the target, step by step. The DCF gives Rp1,803 a share today. Rolled forward twelve months at the 17.4% cost of equity and net of the Rp58 of dividends expected over that period, the base case is Rp2,059. The three scenarios are then weighted 30.0% bear, 50.0% base and 20.0% bull, at Rp316, Rp2,059 and Rp4,404, which gives Rp2,005. The engine applies a 20.0% discount for the illiquid register and the IDR203.0m of average daily turnover, which gives the Rp1,604 target, and the dividend of Rp58 takes the total return to 87.8% [S0]. That is the number behind the BUY rating. The dividend-capacity anchor — 6.5% on our FY2026E payout — is what makes the wait bearable while the re-rating closes.

The first risk is the cycle. The nine-month gross margin of 18.5% is well above the FY2025 trough of 15.7% and above the four-year average, and it was earned while chemical prices were rising [S2][S5]. A distributor earns inventory gains when prices rise and inventory losses when they fall; the same margin that expanded on the way up compresses on the way down, and the operating leverage that produced the earnings increase works in reverse. Our bear case gives back two of those margin points, halves revenue growth, lifts the cost of debt and weakens the rupiah, and on those assumptions the value is Rp316 — below today's Rp885. That is the point of this revision: the downside is a loss, not a lull [S0].

The second is import competition and trade policy. The plastics and petrochemical association says its members are under pressure from cheaper imports and has asked for safeguard and anti-dumping action, and the government has promised standards and trade remedies [S12]. For Lautan Luas the transmission is through the price of the commodity end of its range and through inventory values; a safeguard would help domestic producers but could raise the cost of imported product the distributor sells. The direction of policy is uncertain in both directions, which is why we treat it as a risk rather than a forecast.

The third is refinancing and liquidity. Short-term bank loans of IDR860.4bn and bonds of IDR419.2bn classified as current, against current assets of IDR4,136.2bn and current liabilities of IDR3,586.5bn, mean the company is relying on rolling bank lines and on the bond market at the same time [S6]. The Rp135bn maturity in November 2026 and the Rp286bn maturity in July 2027 are small against the asset base but large against the free cash flow of a working-capital-heavy year [S5]. If the refinancing is done at a materially higher rate than the coupons now in issue, the interest line rises and the equity value falls [S5]. The base case assumes refinancing in place at the 9.0% cost of debt the model carries; the bear case reprices the whole stack at a materially higher rate and cuts the value accordingly, which is where the risk is priced.

The fourth is the associate book. Associates carried at IDR653.3bn generated losses of IDR44.3bn in FY2025 and IDR52.4bn in the nine months of 2026, and the company impaired one of them in both periods [S5][S6]. If the losses continue, the carrying value is at risk and the equity bridge in our valuation overstates value by the amount of any further impairment. Our base case carries the associate loss at -70bn a year in every forecast year — the annualised nine-month run rate — because the impairment the company took in 2026 sits inside other operating expenses above the operating line and cannot offset the below-the-line share of losses [S6]. The bridge carries the associates at zero, so the value we ascribe to them is already net of the losses we forecast; what it does not carry is a cash injection into the associates, which would be worse than our bear.

The fifth is the minority leakage. Minorities took a much larger share of profit in the nine months of 2026 than in FY2025, because the manufacturing subsidiaries where they sit are the ones that recovered [S5][S6]. If manufacturing keeps outgrowing distribution, the parent's share of group profit grows more slowly than group profit, and the value per share is lower than a group-level model implies. We have priced that rather than noted it: the deduction in the bridge is the capitalised value of the minority's share of the operating business, not its book, so a further shift toward manufacturing does not re-open the gap unless the share itself rises [S6].

The sixth is governance and control. The controlling shareholder holds 56.6% and the public 36.1%, with 6.1% in treasury stock, which means the market for the shares is thin, the price can move on small flows, and a minority holder has limited influence [S10]. Related-party balances are small relative to the balance sheet — trade receivables from related parties of IDR10.0bn against IDR1,804.6bn from third parties — but the group structure is layered and the associates are related parties, so the risk is one of valuation rather than of outright expropriation [S6].

The seventh is currency. The rupiah is at Rp18,228/USD against the dollar, weaker than the FY2026E average in the macro deck of Rp17,570/USD, and the group imports a large share of what it distributes [d.macro][S7]. A weaker rupiah raises the cost of imported product and the working capital needed to carry it; pass-through is high but lagged, so a sharp move hits one or two quarters of margin. The model carries 35.0% of cost of goods sold as rupiah-exposed with 90.0% of any move passed through in price, and the bear case applies a five per cent depreciation to it [S5][d.macro].

The signposts we would watch are the quarterly gross margin, where a fall back toward the FY2025 level would confirm the cycle has turned; the working capital cycle, where a reversal from 52.0 days would signal that growth is being bought with credit; the terms of the bond refinancing; and any safeguard or anti-dumping decision [S2][S5][S12]. The third quarter's 17.3% against 20.7% in the second is exactly the line to watch: one step down from a high base, attributed by the company to distribution, is not yet the compression that would move us; a second quarter at or below the third quarter's rate with revenue flat would be.

Ownership and control are concentrated and stable. PT Caturkarsa Megatunggal is the immediate parent and the ultimate parent of the group and holds 56.6% of the shares; the two directors on the register hold 0.6% and 0.6%, treasury stock is 6.1% and the public holds 36.1% [S10]. The public stake is thin enough that the engine's liquidity discount of 20.0% is a fair reflection of what a minority holder could realise, though the discount is set by the traded-value schedule rather than by the ownership percentages [S0]. There is no evidence of a change of control, a tender or a group restructuring in the period we cover.

On disclosure and audit, the FY2025 accounts were audited by KAP Purwanto Susanti dan Surja, a member firm of the Ernst & Young global network, with an unqualified opinion [S5]. The annual report states that neither the company, its subsidiaries, nor any serving commissioner or director was involved in a civil or criminal case, an arbitration, a tax dispute or a bankruptcy or debt-suspension proceeding in 2025, and that no material administrative sanction was imposed [S10]. That is the clean end of the disclosure range for an Indonesian small cap.

Related-party dealings are modest on the face of the balance sheet. Trade receivables from related parties were IDR10.0bn at the end of September 2026 against IDR1,804.6bn from third parties, and trade payables to related parties IDR23.5bn against IDR1,668.7bn to third parties [S6]. The associate book of IDR653.3bn is the larger related-party exposure, because the associates are part of the group's water and chemicals network [S6]. The risk here is valuation rather than diversion: related-party sales and purchases are disclosed at arm's length and are small relative to the group.

The dividend record is steady but cyclical. Dividends per share were Rp50 for FY2022, Rp35 for FY2023, Rp45 for FY2024 and Rp31 for FY2025, so the payout moves with earnings rather than being fixed [S5][S7]. The buyback that ended in February 2025 repurchased 90.2m shares, a meaningful return of capital for a company of this size, at an average price above the current market [S10]. A company that buys its own shares above today's price is either confident in the cycle or was wrong about it; the subsequent earnings recovery suggests the former, but it also reduced the free float.

On ESG, the group's manufacturing subsidiaries carry the environmental exposure that a chemicals business carries: effluent, hazardous materials handling and energy use. The disclosed record is compliance rather than leadership. PT Lautan Luas received an EcoVadis sustainability assessment committed badge in October 2025, PT Dunia Kimia Jaya received the same badge in August 2025 and a gold Indonesia Responsible Care Award in October 2025, and the Semarang plant holds a blue, compliant rating under the environment ministry's corporate performance programme [S10]. There is no disclosed emissions target in the materials we hold, and the sustainability report is referenced rather than reproduced. The one new datapoint since the results is operational rather than reported: the group's logistics subsidiary certified its Bekasi warehouse under the EDGE green-building standard, with 27.2% energy efficiency and 55.3% water savings against a conventional build [S14]. That is a cost line and a customer credential, not a valuation item, but it is the kind of disclosure that answers the supply-chain emissions questionnaires the food and personal-care customers are starting to send. For a distributor and specialty manufacturer the transition risk is moderate: the products themselves are not the source of a large direct carbon liability, and the water-treatment business is a positive exposure to the transition rather than a negative one.

For a company of this kind the material governance questions are the ones that do not show up in a compliance statement: whether the controlling family treats the listed entity as the primary vehicle or as one asset among several, whether related-party transactions are priced at arm's length, and whether the board has the independence to challenge a related-party deal. The clean audit opinion and the small related-party balances answer the second question for now; the concentration of ownership answers the first, in the sense that minority holders are passengers rather than drivers.

The nearest dated catalyst is the November 2026 maturity of the Rp135bn series B bond, which falls this month. The company says it has scheduled the payment, and no repayment or refinancing announcement had been published when this note was written; the terms on which it refinances the bond, or replaces it with bank lines, will tell us what the market is charging for its credit [S5][S9]. The second is the July 2027 maturity of the Rp286bn 2024 series bonds, which is the larger test and the one that sets the interest cost in our forecast [S5].

The results calendar is the other set of dates. The FY2026 audited accounts and annual report, expected around April 2027, will be the first full-year set that carries the restated depreciation base and a full year of the nine-month margin gains, and they will show whether the fourth quarter held [S5][S7]. Before that, the quarterly trading updates give the margin and working capital cycle, which are the two lines that decide whether the base case or the bear case is right [S2].

On policy, any safeguard or anti-dumping decision affecting petrochemicals and plastics imports is a catalyst in both directions, and the industry association's lobbying makes a decision plausible within our horizon [S12]. On capital returns, the dividend for FY2026 will be proposed at the annual meeting in 2027, and the payout of 30.0% we assume is the level the company has held through the cycle [S5][S7].

The KPIs we monitor between updates are the gross margin, the working capital cycle, the EBITDA to interest cover, the net debt to EBITDA ratio and the minority share of profit [S2][S7]. The first two tell us whether the cycle is holding; the last three tell us whether the balance sheet and the group structure are helping or hurting the equity holder.
